summary: Defines domain-based service names and a matching name type for GSS-API, and covers internationalization of the API. A domain-based name identifies a service by the domain it serves, which helps clients authorize clustered servers even when service discovery is not secure. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of trusting a single server's name, you trust whoever serves your company's domain. That way a fake helper found by an unsafe search is easier to spot.

questions: what is a domain based name type
what is a gss-api domain-based name
how does gss-api handle internationalized domain names
subtitle: A GSS-API name type that names a service by the domain it serves, plus Unicode-aware name functions.

tldr.problem: Clients often find servers through insecure lookups such as DNS SRV queries, and can be redirected to a wrong or malicious server that still holds valid credentials under its own name.
tldr.mechanism: A domain-based name has the form service@domain@hostname, so a server that holds credentials for the domain-based service name is thereby authorized to serve that domain. The RFC also adds UTF-8 variants of the import and display functions for internationalized domain names.
tldr.outcome: Clients can authorize clustered servers by authenticating their service names, without securing discovery or running a second authorization protocol.

today: RFC 5178 is a Proposed Standard from May 2008, and the unit metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why Domain-Based Names
sections.content:
Some methods of server discovery are insecure, for example DNS SRV queries made without DNSSEC. A client can be redirected to an incorrect and possibly malicious server, even one that has credentials for itself and can authenticate to the client.

Domain-based names let a GSS-API initiator (the client) authorize acceptors (servers) for a resource without securing discovery and without an additional protocol for server authorization. Either a discovered server has credentials for the domain-based service names it is meant to answer, or it does not, and having valid credentials embodies its authorization to provide the domain-wide service.

A domain-based name has three required elements: a service name, a domain name and a hostname. The domain name and hostname should be DNS names, though the names could be used in non-DNS environments. The RFC adds that the idea is not new: it cites at least one LDAP implementation and the DIGEST-MD5 mechanism as using similar notions.
sections.plainLanguage: If a stranger says they are a company helper, you cannot be sure. If they hold the company's official badge, you can. Domain-based names are that badge check for computers.

sections.title: Name Syntax and Examples
sections.content:
There is a single syntax for domain-based names, written in ABNF: domain-based-name = service "@" domain "@" hostname. The hostname follows the same rules as a domain, which is a series of dot-separated sub-domains made of letters, digits and hyphens. The service part is defined in Section 4.1 of RFC 2743.

The non-normative examples are ldap@somecompany.example@ds1.somecompany.example and nfs@somecompany.example@nfsroot1.somecompany.example. In each, the middle part is the domain being served and the last part is the particular server.
sections.plainLanguage: The name reads like "job, at company, at desk": what the server does, which domain it serves, and which machine it is.

sections.title: The New Name Type
sections.content: The document creates a new GSS-API name type with the symbolic name GSS_C_NT_DOMAINBASED_SERVICE. Its OID is {iso(1) org(3) dod(6) internet(1) security(5) nametypes(6) gss-domain-based(5)}. IANA has recorded it as value 5, gss-domain-based-services, in the name-type registry.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a new kind of name tag, registered in an official list so everyone uses the same tag.

sections.title: Internationalization
sections.content:
Because domain names can be internationalized, the RFC introduces new versions of GSS_Import_name() and GSS_Display_name() to support Unicode. It also allows ACE-encoded DNS names in the existing non-internationalized interfaces.

When importing with the domain-based name type, GSS_Import_name() implementations and mechanisms MUST accept ACE-encoded internationalized domain names in the hostname and domain slots. A new function, GSS_Import_name_utf8(), SHOULD also be provided. It works like the original but MUST accept internationalized names both as UTF-8 strings and as ACE-encoded strings.

For display, GSS_Display_name() MUST output only US-ASCII or ACE-encoded names in those slots. A new GSS_Display_name_utf8() SHOULD also exist and outputs UTF-8 strings, and it MUST NOT output ACE-encoded names.
sections.plainLanguage: Some web names use letters from many languages. The old functions write them in a plain keyboard-safe code, while the new ones can read and write the real letters.

sections.title: Application Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives two non-normative scenarios from its authors. In NFSv4, clients building a domain-wide namespace would find root servers with DNS SRV lookups, without DNSSEC where it is not deployed. When using RPCSEC_GSS, they would use domain-based names to confirm that the servers named in the SRV records are really authorized to be the root servers for the target domain.

LDAP clients using GSS-API through SASL could benefit in the same way. Unlike NFSv4 clients, they do not always know from context when to use domain-based names, because existing clients may use host-based naming. Switching them before servers have domain-based credentials would break interoperability, so LDAP clients may need extra configuration at deployment time to enable or disable the feature.
sections.plainLanguage: A file-sharing client and a directory client can both look up servers in an unsafe phone book. The badge check afterwards makes sure they only talk to servers that truly belong to their company.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Some GSS-API mechanisms may not be able to negotiate domain-based names, and some acceptors may not support them. Initiators then fall back to host-based names, and in that case they MUST also verify that the acceptor's host-based name is authorized to provide the service for the domain they wanted. The same applies to any initiator that lacks support for domain-based service names.

The existence of a domain-based service name conveys meaningful information that initiators may use for authorization decisions. Administrators of distributed authentication services should therefore understand the significance of the service names for which they create acceptor credentials.
sections.plainLanguage: If a server has no company badge, you cannot use the badge check. You then have to find another way to be sure it is allowed to speak for the company.

data.title: Domain-based name syntax
data.code:
domain-based-name = service "@" domain "@" hostname

hostname          = domain

domain            = sub-domain 1*("." sub-domain)

sub-domain        = Let-dig [Ldh-str]

Let-dig           = ALPHA / DIGIT

Ldh-str           = *( ALPHA / DIGIT / "-" ) Let-dig
